rationale: The book's core identification of 'justify/justification' as judging, declaring, or demonstrating a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge (opposite of condemn) unifies every supplied use without contradiction or imported technical terms, while its secondary elaborations correctly distinguish God's gracious forgiveness of the ungodly (via Christ) from any renaming of ungodliness as righteousness and from deeds that can only vindicate rather than purchase. This outperforms the common forensic-soteriological reading (declaration of imputed righteousness for the sinner by faith alone), which cannot non-analogically cover the non-salvific and non-human-object uses that the book treats as definitional.
book_core_identification: To judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge (opposite of condemn).
book_secondary_elaborations: God answers the charge against the sinner by grace through Christ, forgiving rather than renaming ungodliness righteousness.
Deeds may vindicate a claimed faith (as with Abraham and Rahab), but they cannot purchase the Judge's mercy or place God in debt.
The courtroom/legal frame from Deut 25:1 and Prov 17:15 supplies the base sense that then extends to words, wisdom, God, and self-justification claims.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The common Protestant forensic reading: justification is God's legal/courtroom declaration that a sinner is righteous (acquitted and counted righteous by imputation of Christ's righteousness) on the basis of faith in Christ rather than works, with other uses treated as secondary, analogical, or demonstrative senses (e.g., James).
counter_core_identification: God's forensic declaration that a sinner is righteous/acquitted and counted righteous by faith in Christ (imputed righteousness), as the central soteriological act.
material_core_denial: The counter narrows the judicial sense to a specialized soteriological act of imputing righteousness to ungodly sinners, treating non-salvific or non-human uses (justifying God, wisdom, words, self) as secondary or figurative rather than definitional; the book denies that the core is restricted to imputation or sinner-acquittal and insists the general judicial sense must govern all uses first.
counter_case: Romans 3:24-26; 4:4-8; 5:1,9,16-19; 8:33 frame justification as God's free gracious act through Christ's blood/redemption that answers the charge against the elect and produces peace, with faith counted as righteousness and sin not imputed.
Galatians 2:16; 3:6-14 and Philippians 3:9 contrast justification by faith in Christ with works of the law, supporting a forensic transfer of status rather than mere demonstration.

Theological tradition (classic Protestant) and parallel texts (2 Cor 5:21; Titus 3:5-7) treat the term as technical for the declarative act of counting the believer righteous, with James 2:21-25 as a distinct demonstrative sense of works proving genuine faith.
Deut 25:1 and Prov 17:15 establish the legal backdrop that Paul then specializes for the gospel of the ungodly being justified.
book_explanatory_advantages: Single uniform sense covers all printed references without exception or special pleading: Deut 25:1/Prov 17:15 (judges), Matt 11:19 (wisdom), Luke 7:29 (people justify God), Rom 3:4 (God justified in sayings), Matt 12:37 (words), Luke 10:29/16:15 (self-justification claims), James 2:21-25 (Abraham/Rahab by works as demonstration), and the Pauline soteriological uses (Rom 3:24-26; 4:5-8; 8:33).

Preserves the integrity of 'justifies the ungodly' as forgiveness of iniquities/covering of sins/non-imputation (Rom 4:5-8) without requiring God to rename wrong-living as right-living, consistent with prior findings on righteousness.

Distinguishes cleanly from sanctification and cleansing (1 Cor 6:11) as answering different questions (verdict vs. ownership/appointment vs. defilement removal), avoiding collapse into transformative or progressive moral improvement.

Aligns with prior adjudicated cores (faith as trusting faithfulness enacted in obedience; works as deeds not synonymous with obedience or purchase price; works of the law as deeds that cannot purchase; righteousness as right-living never renamed wrong).
Requires no extra technical apparatus of imputation as definitional; the mechanism is secondary to the judicial act itself.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Captures the dominant Pauline soteriological cluster (Rom 3-5, 8; Gal 2-3) with high density and theological precision for the gospel of free justification of the ungodly by faith.
Fits classic Protestant systematic summaries and the contrast with condemnation/works of the law.
Handles James by a well-attested distinction between declarative (Paul) and demonstrative (James) senses.
decisive_sources: Deut 25:1 and Prov 17:15 (base judicial pair justify/condemn the righteous/wicked)
Luke 7:29 (people justified God) and Matt 11:19 (wisdom justified by her children)
Rom 3:4 (God justified in his sayings); Rom 4:5-8 (justifies the ungodly = sins forgiven/covered/not imputed, not renamed)
James 2:21-25 (Abraham/Rahab justified by works as faith made perfect/visible)
Prior findings on faith, works, works of the law, and righteousness
unresolved_objections: Whether the forensic soteriological uses in Paul require 'imputation of Christ's righteousness' as an indispensable mechanism rather than a secondary description of the gracious verdict/forgiveness.
How precisely final/eschatological judgment according to works (e.g., Rom 2; 2 Cor 5:10) interfaces with present justification without becoming a second purchase price.
